title: arXiv AI daily — Thursday, 19 November 2026
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart, and this is an inferred, relevance-weighted shortlist rather than a popularity ranking; independent attention and citation evidence are limited for such recent papers.

sections.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
sections.abstract: TwinLab-Bench tests agents designing their own experiments across 52 real-laboratory-derived tasks, using lab-record-grounded digital twins and reports to score results; the strongest tested model averaged 45.0/100.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce task-specific TwinLab agents that return recorded or calculated experimental readings, and report that the best of 13 tested agents scores 45.0/100; the paper also analyzes common experiment-design failures.
sections.unique_caveat: The benchmark tests agents in constructed digital twins, not by conducting new physical experiments; its readings and scoring are grounded in the records and calculators assembled for 52 tasks.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Independent coverage at Emergent and AGI Hunt, a public GitHub benchmark and Hugging Face paper discussion; its three-way cross-list within the core AI corpus gives it unusually broad category relevance.

sections.title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
sections.abstract: PhyDEX evaluates whether robot policies can infer object mass, center of mass, and friction to throw objects to targets, reporting sub-3% success for three tested VLA policies.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors provide 35,357 simulated trajectories across nine throwing tasks and 100 scenes, with humanoid and real-world tests; they report that providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles policy success.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors explicitly limit the benchmark to throwing, three randomized physical properties, and three VLA policies; they call for richer physics, more skills, and broader model coverage.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Independent discussion from Data Phoenix and a technical critique at Pith; the arXiv abstract and full text make its evaluation setup and limits checkable. Attention indicators are qualitative, not a readership measure.

sections.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
sections.abstract: AutoMaster uses natural-language skills, trajectory analysis, and data selection to shape teacher demonstrations before fine-tuning a target model, reporting gains over vanilla supervised fine-tuning across six settings.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report that Skill-FT improves mean performance over vanilla SFT by 1.42–8.99 percentage points on Terminal, Search, and software-engineering tasks, holding teacher, task pool, training-set size, and SFT recipe fixed.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported experiments use Qwen3.5 4B/9B target models and six settings across three task families; transfer to other model families, teachers, or tasks remains to be demonstrated.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The authors provide a public project page, code, and model release; a Hugging Face paper page and multi-benchmark result add checkable technical evidence. These indicate dissemination and relevance, not verified popularity.

sections.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
sections.abstract: AgentRoboCritic pairs each robot action with the agent’s stated local intent so a critic can label its outcome and failure mode, analyzing frontier agents across 12 manipulation benchmarks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report that fine-tuning Muse-Glimmer-30B raises failure-mode accuracy from 32.58% to 74.24% on their 400-action human-annotated benchmark, enabling lower-cost action-level analysis.
sections.unique_caveat: Critic validation is based on 400 human-annotated actions; generalization to other robots, action distributions, and independently annotated evaluation sets remains open.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Its cross-list spans three core AI categories, and the authors released a 12,844-action dataset and critic project with a human-annotated evaluation set. This is a concrete artifact, but outside-attention evidence is sparse, so placement is relevance-led.

sections.title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
sections.abstract: JARVIS uses an embodied agent and executable digital twin to design, fabricate, measure, and revise circuit boards, demonstrating a 60 Hz notch filter built and tested without human intervention.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report an end-to-end design–build–test–learn loop using unmodified desktop equipment, with a robot arm, PCB printer, pick-and-place machine, digital-twin rehearsal, and hardware-in-the-loop circuit tests.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported physical result is one first-run 60 Hz notch-filter experiment; it does not establish repeatability across board types, component failures, or longer production runs.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The paper is indexed with paper/code information by CatalyzeX and ArXivSignals. These are modest discovery signals rather than independent popularity measures; lower placement reflects limited external attention and one demonstrated circuit task.
